title: Prefetch throttle and fallback ladder: memory deferral and graceful recovery
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem statement: We continue to see tight GPU memory pressure when continuous-batching interacts with aggressive KV prefetch. In tail cases a single large request that triggers many KV entries plus long sequence length can push a serving pod into OOM despite existing tiered-eviction logic. Current fallbacks trigger model swaps or hard rejects which produce poor client latency and quality degradation.

Goal: Design and implement a graceful memory-deferral and fallback ladder that: (1) throttles KV prefetch per-request based on admission/priority, (2) supports partial response streaming while deferring exact-KV population (token-level deferral), (3) provides a deterministic fallback ladder (quantized model -> smaller-context variant -> CPU fallback) with bounded retry/backoff, and (4) integrates with the batching admission controller and Console observability for SLO/outcome attribution.

Scope: runtime + serving admission controller + Console dashboarding + unit/e2e tests. Not in scope: model architecture changes.

Design overview:
- Admission controller extension: add a "prefetch_budget" derived from per-pod memory headroom and current KV pressure. Requests carry priority tags; controller can accept fully, accept-with-prefetch-throttle, or route to fallback ladder.
- Token-level deferral: allow the runtime to stream partial outputs while marking some token positions as "deferred-kv". Deferred KV entries are loaded opportunistically after first byte streaming completes or during idle GPU cycles. This reduces peak concurrent KV memory.
- Fallback ladder: deterministic ordered fallbacks per request: full-fp16 -> int8-quant variant (same architecture) -> truncated-context variant (reduce prefix retention) -> smaller-architecture model -> CPU-heap fallback (best-effort). Each fallback step has a max-retries and exponential backoff tuned to avoid stampedes.
- Memory compaction hooks: trigger async device-side compaction when moving between models in the ladder. Expose compaction cost/benefit in telemetry.
- Admission backpressure signals: expose a 'soft-shed' metric and API header so clients/SDKs can adaptively lower request concurrency or reduce prefix length.

Trade-offs considered:
- Partial streaming with deferred KV may increase latency for later tokens when deferred-populate happens; mitigated by opportunistic background population and prioritizing near-deferred tokens.
- CPU fallback avoids OOM but is much slower; we cap per-customer CPU fallback rate and record fallback-sla metrics.
- More complex ladder increases surface area for bugs; implement in incrementally gated feature flag with canary rollout.

Acceptance criteria:
- Admission controller respects prefetch_budget and can publish decisions to Console.
- End-to-end integration test demonstrating a crafted high-KV tail request results in one ladder fallback step lower (e.g., quantized model) rather than OOM, with client receiving partial stream + final completion without hard error.
- Console shows new metrics: prefetch_budget, deferred_kv_count, fallback_step, fallback_latency_penalty.
- Benchmark: 95th percentile error-on-request due to OOM reduced by >= 80% for a synthetic high-KV workload compared to baseline.

Implementation plan (high level):
1) Spec admission controller API and new headers (1 week).
2) Implement prefetch_budget computation and enforcement in admission controller (2 weeks).
3) Runtime: token-deferral flags, deferred-kv queue, opportunistic loader, and compaction hooks (3 weeks).
4) Fallback ladder orchestration with retry/backoff and async telemetry (2 weeks).
5) Integrations: Console telemetry, SDK header semantics, and canary rollout plan (2 weeks).
6) Tests, load validation, and gradual rollout (2 weeks).

Open design questions:
- Should deferred KV population be prioritized by token distance from stream head or by token attention weight? (Prefer distance-first for simplicity.)
- How aggressive should prefetch_budget be under noisy neighbors vs. single-tenant Dedicated nodes? (Expose config per deployment tier.)
- What's the safe default for per-tenant CPU-fallback rate? (Propose 0.1% of requests as initial cap.)

Links and artifacts:
- Design draft: https://redwood-internal.confluence/display/RUN/Prefetch+Throttle+Design (internal)
- Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4381
- Load harness: https://internal-builds.redwood.ai/oom-harness/2026-03-presubmit

Rollout strategy: start with internal canary on non-prod fleet, then staged rollout to 5% Hosted traffic, monitor fallback metrics and latency; then 25% and 100% if stable. Feature gated by runtime-1.25 flag 'prefetch_throttle_v1'.
comments: 2026-03-10 Aisha Patel: Ticket created after two customer incidents last week. Initial design draft uploaded to Confluence.
2026-03-11 Miguel Alvarez: Spike implemented for deferred-kv queue. Early bench shows 40% reduction in peak GPU mem during synthetic test. Results in PR 4381.
2026-03-11 Priya Nair (SRE): Suggested adding async device compaction hook and exposing compaction cost metric to Console. Added to design.
2026-03-12 Daniel Cho (PM): Asked to limit customer-visible quality regression; set CPU-fallback cap to 0.1% by default and require per-customer opt-in for higher caps.
2026-03-12 Miguel Alvarez: Implemented admission header 'X-Redwood-Prefetch-Mode' and 'X-Redwood-Prefetch-Budget'. Pushed experimental flag to canary cluster.
2026-03-12 QA: Added e2e case to the harness to validate partial-stream + deferred completion for long-context requests. Failing intermittently — investigating race in deferred-kv popper.
